subject: My data unsuitable for SEM analysis?

messages.subject: My data unsuitable for SEM analysis?
parts:
Dear all,

I am trying to apply SEM (for the first time) to my graduate research, and I have been learning about SEM and lavaan from online resources and examples, but when it comes to my own research, I am having some difficulties that I am not sure how to solve.

This is my sample model (all are continuous variables, except for C1 and C2 which are categorical variables with 0s and 1s) and the associated error messages:

samplemodel<-'
# latent variables
H =~ c1 + c2 + x1
A =~ x2 + x3 
D =~ x4 + x5 
PR =~ x6 + x7
PS =~ x8 + x9 + x10
# regressions
PR ~ H
A ~ PR + H
D ~ PR + H
PS ~ PR + A + D
'

samplemodelSEM<-sem(samplemodel,data=sample)

Warning messages:
1: In lavSampleStatsFromData(Data = lavaanData, missing = lavaanOptions$missing,  :
  lavaan WARNING: sample covariance can not be inverted
2: In estimateVCOV(lavaanModel, samplestats = lavaanSampleStats, options = lavaanOptions,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!

3: In lavaan(model = samplemodel, data = sample, model.type = "sem",  :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated variances are negative
4: In lavaan(model = samplemodel, data = sample, model.type = "sem",  :

5: In lavaan(model = samplemodel, data = sample, model.type = "sem",  :

Attached are a drawing of what I hypothesized the relationships in the model to behave and the sample dataset that yielded the result above.  When I create a covariance matrix of the variables in my model (see below), the values are quite low.  Is it because of the weak covariances that are affecting my model or is my model syntax incorrect that is causing the problems?

messages.subject: Re: My data unsuitable for SEM analysis?
parts:
Hi Peter,

The first warning indicates that your sample covariance matrix can't be inverted.  This has nothing to do with the fitted model, so you can look for problems in the sample covariance a couple of ways.  You could use the cov2cor() function to standardize the covariance matrix, and look for any out-of-bounds values or indications of redundancy between two variables.  But it might be a case of multicollinearity (i.e., one variable is redundant with a linear combination of 2 or more other variables), which you probably wouldn't be able to notice in a correlation matrix.  In your case, it turns out that the 2 categorical variables are completely redundant with each other: c2 = -(c1 - 1), so they are perfectly negatively correlated:

> round(cov2cor(cov(dat)), 3)
        c1     c2     x1     x2     x3     x4     x5     x6     x7     x8     x9    x10
c1   1.000 -1.000 -0.764  0.054  0.071 -0.142 -0.347 -0.005 -0.135 -0.154 -0.058 -0.098
c2  -1.000  1.000  0.764 -0.054 -0.071  0.142  0.347  0.005  0.135  0.154  0.058  0.098
x1  -0.764  0.764  1.000  0.092 -0.315  0.122  0.072  0.018 -0.047  0.156  0.100  0.156
x2   0.054 -0.054  0.092  1.000 -0.101  0.535  0.008  0.106 -0.162  0.128  0.170  0.240
x3   0.071 -0.071 -0.315 -0.101  1.000 -0.016  0.553  0.027 -0.075 -0.120 -0.043 -0.040
x4  -0.142  0.142  0.122  0.535 -0.016  1.000 -0.008  0.088 -0.080  0.032  0.148  0.215
x5  -0.347  0.347  0.072  0.008  0.553 -0.008  1.000  0.008  0.214 -0.023  0.177  0.177
x6  -0.005  0.005  0.018  0.106  0.027  0.088  0.008  1.000 -0.029  0.147 -0.169 -0.150
x7  -0.135  0.135 -0.047 -0.162 -0.075 -0.080  0.214 -0.029  1.000 -0.127  0.152  0.037
x8  -0.154  0.154  0.156  0.128 -0.120  0.032 -0.023  0.147 -0.127  1.000 -0.017  0.051
x9  -0.058  0.058  0.100  0.170 -0.043  0.148  0.177 -0.169  0.152 -0.017  1.000  0.817
x10 -0.098  0.098  0.156  0.240 -0.040  0.215  0.177 -0.150  0.037  0.051  0.817  1.000
> table(dat$c1, dat$c2)
  
      0   1
  0   0 100
  1  90   0

So you only need one of those to define your H construct.  (By the way, in the path diagram, the factor loadings need to point in the other direction; i.e., latent factors predict observe variables, not the other way around).  I don't see a problem with inverting the sample covariance matrix if you take out c1 (or c2), because the determinant would then be positive:

> det(cov(dat[ , -1]))
[1] 7.402503e-08
However, you have a categorical indicator (c1 or c2), and you might consider treating x4 and x5 as categorical since they only have 4-5 levels, respectively, so might not be approximately normal.  So you should treat it as such by indicating the name(s) of the categorical indicators in the sem() function:

sem(model, data, ordered = c("c2", "x4", "x5"))

I couldn't get that model to converge either, though, and I think the fact that your within-construct correlations are so low is problematicwith the exception of H.  Essentially, either the fundamental assumption of your measurement model don't hold (i.e., these indicators don't measure the same thing), or the indicators measure mostly noise relative to the actual latent construct you are trying to measure:

> cor(dat[, 2:3])
          c2        x1
c2 1.0000000 0.7640471
x1 0.7640471 1.0000000

> cor(dat[, 4:5])
           x2         x3
x2  1.0000000 -0.1012089
x3 -0.1012089  1.0000000

> cor(dat[, 6:7])
             x4           x5
x4  1.000000000 -0.008364336
x5 -0.008364336  1.000000000

> cor(dat[, 8:9])
            x6          x7
x6  1.00000000 -0.02862939
x7 -0.02862939  1.00000000

> cor(dat[, 10:12])
             x8          x9        x10
x8   1.00000000 -0.01673414 0.05141167
x9  -0.01673414  1.00000000 0.81732918
x10  0.05141167  0.81732918 1.00000000


Terry

Thank you, Terry, for giving me feedback and explaining what was wrong.

I have been struggling the last few days trying to remove the less ecologically-important variables to get the SEM to work.

I came up with the following model which produced no error messages.  Unfortunately, the chi-square p-value was 0.000 (and thus the model was a poor fit).

sample<-read.csv("sample.csv",header=T)

H =~ x1
    A =~ 1*x2
    D =~ 1*x4
    PR =~ 1*x6
    PS =~ 1*x8 + 1*x9 + 1*x10

# regressions
    PR ~ H
    A ~ PR + H
    D ~ PR + H
    PS ~ PR + A + D
    '

samplemodelSEM<-sem(samplemodel,data=sample)

summary(samplemodelSEM)

I looked through some posts here regarding modeling fit but couldn't find anything suggesting how to improve the model fit.  Do I require more trial-and-errors to find a better-fit model?  Thanks again.

Peter

------------------

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: My data unsuitable for SEM analysis?
parts:
There's a lot of controversy about how to evaluate a model, too much to really get into here.  But there are other fit indices lavaan provides that can help you determine whether the differences between your observed and model-implied covariances are of any practical importance.  Also, I like to see exactly which covariances are not being adequately reproduced by the model.  You can see which standardized residuals are particularly large (I've heard rules of thumb that any greater than +/- 0.1 are a sign of trouble):

resid(samplemodelSEM, type = "standardized")

Any covariances that the model isn't reproducing adequately means that there might need to be a free path between those two variables.

Terry

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: My data unsuitable for SEM analysis?
parts:
On 10/07/2013 08:08 PM, PSYL wrote:
> samplemodel<-'
> # latent variables
> H =~ x1
> A =~ 1*x2
> D =~ 1*x4
> PR =~ 1*x6
> PS =~ 1*x8 + 1*x9 + 1*x10

For the PS latent variable: do you really want to constrain the 'factor
loadings' of x9 and x10 to 1?

> I looked through some posts here regarding modeling fit but couldn't
> find anything suggesting how to improve the model fit.

To explore model misfit, you can look at the modification indices:

modindices(samplemodelSEM)

But remember: they only reflect model misfit in your particular sample.

Yves.
